title: The weakest pillar
hookLine: every believer has one pillar to strengthen

cards: An old house rarely announces which beam is tired. It drops hints. A door that sticks in summer.
A hairline crack above a window. A floor that rolls a marble toward one corner. A house isn't mended by admiring the parts that hold.
The repair starts the day someone follows the marble. So, of the five pillars, which one is your sticking door? Today, the weakest pillar.

teach.b: In a report in Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ names the five: testifying that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is His messenger, establishing the prayer, giving zakat, the Hajj, and fasting Ramadan.
Five supports for one building. A building with one weak support still stands, and it's still worth attending to. Second, the size of the ask.
The last verse of the Qur'an's second surah, in Pickthall's words: "Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope." The question isn't how to be flawless by Friday. It's what's within reach this week.
Third, the size of the step.
In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet is asked which deeds are most loved by Allah, and he says the ones done regularly, even if they are small. A weak pillar is rarely mended by one heroic weekend.
It's mended by something small that keeps happening. One prayer that used to slip, kept on time. A little set aside each month toward zakat, so the reckoning isn't a shock.

For the Hajj, which the Qur'an asks of those who can find a way, maybe learning its rites, or opening a savings jar. For the testimony, saying it once a day, slowly, meaning each word. Fourth, the honest part.
Where a pillar has been missed for a long time, prayers or fasts left undone, the schools of law give detailed answers about making them up, and those answers differ.
That conversation belongs with your own scholar, not an app. This day does something smaller: name the pillar, and choose one step.

how: Some Muslims who want to strengthen a pillar start with one regular, small habit, such as one prayer kept on time, and ask a local scholar or imam about making up prayers or fasts that were missed.

o: the pillar the schools of law rank as least important of the five
a pillar that can be left out for good once the others are strong
the one of the five that slips first, mended by a small regular step

games.q: the weakest pillar — tap the pairs.
p: the end of the Qur'an's second surah
the deeds most loved by Allah

s: the Qur'an says Allah asks of a soul more than it can carry
"Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope" (2:286).
in the hadith, the deeds most loved by Allah are the biggest ones
the Prophet said the ones done regularly, even if they are small.
every school of law gives the same answer about making up long-missed prayers
the schools give detailed answers, and those answers differ; that belongs with a person's own scholar.

games.q: you've found your weakest pillar: the prayer slips most days. what's the step the hadith points toward?
o: pray every prayer perfectly, starting tonight.
keep one prayer on time, and keep it up.
wait until you feel ready to do it all.
games.why: the deeds most loved by Allah are the regular ones, even if small. one prayer kept is a beam that holds.

practice: Go through the five, one at a time: the testimony, the prayer, zakat, the fast, the Hajj, and notice which one makes you want to skip ahead.
Look at it the way a builder looks at a crack, with interest, not blame, and shrink one step for it until it's almost too easy: one prayer, one time of day, a when and a where.
If you pray, ask Allah for help with that one step; if not, just hold the plan steady.

wordCard.voice: The weakest pillar. The one of the five that slips first, and so the one worth strengthening with something small and regular. It closes this block on the pillars. Today's word.

orig.note: the pillars of Islam: a rukn is a pillar or corner support of a building.

carryVoice: Your line: strengthen one. Small and regular, not flawless by Friday. Tomorrow a new block opens: what a hadith is.
